# Development

## Building

```
make                 # src/pysacd/_sacdconv.so, tuned for this CPU
make PORTABLE=1      # generic x86-64; the PCM filters still use AVX2/AVX-512 when the CPU has them
make test-tools      # the test-only DST encoder
make HARDEN=0        # without the hardening flags (sanitizer builds)
```

libFLAC (`flac-devel`) is optional: without it FLAC output is disabled and everything else works.

The engine links the [scarletbook-rs](https://github.com/aclater/scarletbook-rs) C library
statically (see [below](#the-scarletbook-library)). The first `make` downloads it into
`build/scarletbook`; `make clean` keeps that copy, and `make distclean` removes it too.

On Linux the engine is built hardened (`HARDEN=1`, the default):

- compiler flags: `-D_FORTIFY_SOURCE=3 -fstack-protector-strong -fstack-clash-protection`, plus
  `-fcf-protection` on x86;
- linker flags: `-Wl,-z,relro,-z,now,-z,noexecstack`.

The flags live in `override CFLAGS`/`LDFLAGS`, so `make CFLAGS=...` keeps them. The cost is in
[performance](performance.md#hardening).

`_native.py` mirrors the engine's `sc_area_t` and `sc_output_t` structs by hand. When it loads
the library, it checks the engine's ABI version (`SACDCONV_ABI` in `csrc/sacdconv.c`, `ABI` in
`_native.py`), then each struct's size and every field offset. It refuses a library that
doesn't match: rebuild it (`make clean all`). Bump both versions whenever a struct or an
exported signature changes.

## The scarletbook library

pysacd's SACD engine (sector formats, TOC parsing, demultiplexing, DST decoding) is
scarletbook-rs, a clean-room Rust library, used through its C interface (ABI 2) since 0.3.0. The
plan and the reasons are in issue #85. The TOC is read through it (see
[below](#the-toc-through-scarletbook)), and so is the audio
([below](#the-audio-through-scarletbook)). pysacd's own TOC parser, sector demultiplexer and DST
decoder were removed with it; they are in the history up to v0.2.2.

**What is linked.** `scarletbook.lock` pins one scarletbook release: its version, C ABI, commit,
and the SHA-256 of `scarletbook-ffi-<version>-<target>.tar.gz` for every target it is built for.
`tools/scarletbook.py fetch` downloads the archive for the target the C compiler builds for
(`$CC -dumpmachine`), refuses it unless its SHA-256 is the pinned one, and unpacks it. The
Makefile then links `lib/libscarletbook_ffi.a` into `_sacdconv` with the system libraries listed
in the archive's `native-static-libs.txt`.

- **Statically, not as a second shared library.** There is nothing extra to ship, find or load,
  and the per-frame work stays inside one C library: no ctypes call per frame.
- **The whole archive, then only what is exported.** The link takes every member of the archive
  (`--whole-archive`, `-force_load` on macOS), so all of scarletbook's `sb_*` functions are in
  the engine. Python can then call them through ctypes on the same library, as scarletbook's
  README describes. Only those functions and the engine's own `sacdconv_*` functions are exported:
  `csrc/exports.map` on Linux, `csrc/exports.darwin` on macOS, and a `.def` file generated from
  the header and `csrc/sacdconv.c` on Windows. Rust's runtime stays internal, so it can't collide
  with another library in the process, and the linker drops whatever nothing reaches
  (`--gc-sections`, `-dead_strip`).
- **Without Rust's debug information** (`-Wl,-S`), unless `CFLAGS` has `-g`, as the sanitizer
  builds do. It makes up most of the archive's size. The engine grows from about 115 KB to
  about 2.4 MB on x86-64 Linux, and a wheel by about 1 MB.
- **Checked twice.** `csrc/sacdconv.c` refuses at compile time a header whose `SB_ABI_VERSION`
  isn't 2. When the engine loads, `_native.py` refuses it if the linked library's
  `sb_abi_version()` isn't 2 or its `sb_version()` is older than 0.5.4. 0.5.0 is the first
  release with cancellation, progress, and stored and decoded frames in one pass, 0.5.1
  the first with the TOC's timecodes as stored, 0.5.2 the first with the whole TOC in one call
  (`sb_disc_toc`), and 0.5.4 the first whose output API can lay out `sacd_extract`'s DSF and
  DSDIFF files byte for byte (scarletbook-rs#169).
- **Logged.** `_native.build_info()` (in `pysacd --version` and in log files) names the
  scarletbook version, and the debug log carries its full `sb_build_info()`.

**Where the pins come from.** Each pinned archive was downloaded from the release, checked
against the release's own `.sha256` file, and checked with
`gh attestation verify <file> -R aclater/scarletbook-rs`: a signed SLSA build provenance
statement says that scarletbook-rs's release workflow built it from the pinned tag and commit.
CI repeats that check on every pull request, in the `scarletbook provenance` job
(`tools/scarletbook.py attest`, which needs `gh`). The wheel workflow runs it before building
anything. A pin that isn't an attested scarletbook release therefore fails CI, and a build
never uses an archive that doesn't match a pin.

**Building offline, or from scarletbook's source.** `make SCARLETBOOK_DIR=DIR` (or
`SCARLETBOOK_DIR=DIR pip install .`) uses a library already unpacked in DIR, with the release
archive's layout: `include/scarletbook.h`, `lib/libscarletbook_ffi.a` and
`native-static-libs.txt`. Nothing is downloaded. `tools/scarletbook.py fetch --archive FILE`
unpacks a release archive you already have, after the same digest check.
`PYSACD_SCARLETBOOK_CACHE=DIR` keeps downloaded archives there for the next build. For a target
with no release build, build `crates/scarletbook-ffi` with cargo and arrange its static library,
the header and the output of `cargo rustc --crate-type staticlib -- --print native-static-libs`
the same way. Set `SCARLETBOOK_TARGET` when a compiler wrapper misreports its target: Fedora's
`musl-gcc`, for example, says `x86_64-redhat-linux`.

### The TOC through scarletbook

`toc.SACDImage` opens an image with scarletbook (`_sbtoc.SbImage`, `src/pysacd/_sbtoc.py`).
Its `read_sectors()` reads 2048-byte logical sectors whatever the image's sector size
(`sb_disc_read_sectors`), and its `read_toc()` builds the Disc, Area and Track objects.

- **The whole TOC in one call** (#94). `sb_disc_toc` (scarletbook 0.5.2) writes the disc, its
  areas, tracks, text, genres, stored timecodes and warnings into one buffer in a fixed,
  versioned little-endian layout, which `_sbtoc` unpacks with `struct`. It replaced about 100 to
  160 per-field ctypes calls per disc (`sb_disc_string`, `sb_track_info`, ...), which made reading
  a TOC 4.5 times slower than pysacd 0.2's parser (scarletbook-rs#132). The layout's magic,
  major version, size and record sizes are checked, and so is every record and string against
  its end: a layout pysacd can't read is a `SACDError`, never a wrong field. See
  [performance](performance.md#reading-a-toc-in-process-against-a-subprocess).
- **A path is opened by the library** (`sb_disc_open_file`, #94): no Python call per read, which
  was most of what opening an image cost. A caller's file object and a PS3 server
  (`remote.RemoteDisc`) are read through a Python callback (`sb_disc_open_callbacks_at`). If the
  library can't read a path, it is opened in Python instead, so a missing or unreadable file
  raises the `OSError` it always did. A failing read is an `OSError`, an image scarletbook
  rejects a `SACDError`.
- **Checked against the old reader.** `tools/toc_compare.py --old OLD_SRC --new NEW_SRC IMAGE...`
  compares the repr of every Disc, Area and Track and the bytes of `toc --json` between two
  source trees, with `--mutations N` on mutated copies too. The one-call reader matched the
  per-field one of 0.3.0 on the sacd-spec conformance corpus (136 images), the hostile images of
  `tests/sacdgen.py` (95), 3,000 TOC mutations, the 5 real test discs and a library of 291 ISOs
  (271 of them SACDs), and the beets-pysacd fingerprints of all of them were unchanged.
- **The same objects as pysacd 0.2.** Up to 0.2 pysacd had its own parser. Before it was
  removed, the two were compared field by field, on `toc --json` byte for byte, and on the
  beets-pysacd fingerprint (#87). They agreed on the sacd-spec conformance corpus, 3,000 TOC
  mutations, real discs and a library of 142 ISOs. Where scarletbook gives bytes as stored
  (catalogue numbers, language codes, manufacturer data, ISRCs), `_sbtoc` renders them as that
  parser did. The warnings are the specification's codes (see
  [the Python library](library.md#the-parser)).
- **Timecodes as stored.** scarletbook gives play times and track times as frame counts, and,
  since 0.5.1, as stored (`sb_area_playtime_stored`, `sb_track_timecodes_stored`; requested by
  pysacd, [scarletbook-rs#127](https://github.com/aclater/scarletbook-rs/issues/127)). A
  timecode a hostile disc stores out of range, such as `255:255:255`, is written as stored in
  `-P`, cue, XML and DSDIFF markers, as `sacd_extract` and pysacd 0.2 write it. Where
  scarletbook cut a track to the area's play time, its cut count is used, as pysacd's parser
  did.

### The audio through scarletbook

The engine's reader thread (`sb_reader_main` in `csrc/sacdconv.c`) opens the image with
scarletbook, by path, or through the sector source (`sb_disc_open_callbacks_at`) for a PS3. It
finds the area by its TOC's LSN, the one `toc.Area.toc_start` names, and reads the frame range
every output needs as one range (`sb_range_audio_open`). Two frames of context before it and
one after are included, exactly as before, so that PCM output is sample-identical.

- **Decoding in scarletbook's pool.** The range is decoded on a pool of one thread fewer than
  `--threads` (the CPU count by default; at least one) (`sb_pool_new`,
  `sb_track_audio_set_pool`). The reader thread does real work with every frame, staging and
  batching it, and a pool of one thread per CPU plus the reader is one runnable thread more
  than there are CPUs. scarletbook recommends CPUs − 1 for such a caller (scarletbook-rs#146),
  and pysacd measured it as the best of N, N − 1, N − 2 and N − 4 (#94; see
  [performance](performance.md#the-decoding-pool-94)). The engine logs the pool's size at
  debug level. The reader receives every position in order:
  missing ones as 0x69 silence, invalid DST frames as 0x55, the fills pysacd always used. The
  workers lay out DSF and convert to PCM, and the writer is unchanged.
- **Stored and decoded frames in one pass.** When a DSDIFF output keeps DST frames as stored
  (`dff-dst`: the edit master, `-p` without `-c`) next to decoded outputs, the range is read
  with `sb_track_audio_read_with_stored`. When only stored frames are needed, the range is
  read with `sb_raw_frames_read` and nothing is decoded.
- **Past the play time.** scarletbook reads an area's timeline, `[0, play time)`. Positions
  an output asks for beyond it are silence, as they were.
- **Cancellation.** `_native.run_area` calls `sacdconv_cancel()` when its caller is
  interrupted (Ctrl-C, or an exception from the progress callback). That sets the engine's
  flag and requests scarletbook's cancellation token (`SbCancel`), which stops a read within
  32 sectors, the scan before a range's first frame included. `tests/test_engine_scarletbook.py`
  checks that a run reading from a slow source stops within a second.
- **Progress.** The reader copies scarletbook's sector counts (`SbProgress`) into the engine's
  progress fields.
- **ISO copy first.** `-I` copies the image in one sequential pass, as before, and the audio is
  then read from the local copy: a PS3 is read once, and the copy needs no second engine.
- **Logging.** scarletbook's log goes to the `pysacd.engine` logger: its errors as warnings, the
  rest at debug level. pysacd logs missing frames, invalid DST frames and malformed sectors
  itself, from the frame statuses and `sb_track_audio_warning`. The engine also reports the missing frames' count, first and last, and whether the
  area's next-to-last frame is DSD silence, for a workaround (#93): when the only missing frame
  is the area's last, after silence, `pysacd-extract` warns and exits 0. **This is a workaround** for what was seen on early Sony discs (Master TOC 1.00, pressed 2000–2001; four discs of four titles), whose last area sector holds no audio sector header. It may be revisited if other discs show the pattern. See
  [sacd_extract](sacd_extract.md).
- **Provisional starts for ranges far into an area** (`-t`, `convert -t`, `-k`). When an
  output's frames start far into the area, scarletbook starts provisionally
  (`SB_SEEK_POLICY_SPECULATIVE`, with its default gap of 2048 sectors): it finds the range's
  first frame with a short search of the frame timecodes instead of reading the whole area up
  to it.
  - **Why.** Exact reads made `-t` on the last track 4.6× slower than 0.2.2 locally. From a
    network share they cost a read of the area up to the track, up to about 1 GB. On a
    well-formed disc a provisional start is exact by the specification (4.2 item 8), so the
    output is byte-identical to 0.2.2 and `sacd_extract`: 0.2.2 started near the track's LSN
    from the TOC, which no reader can verify either. On a hostile image neither is guaranteed
    exact.
  - **Logged.** The run logs once, at info level, that it started provisionally.
  - **Checked where possible.** With an image file, the area's seek index is kept, and a clone
    of the disc checks the provisional start in the background (`sb_disc_seek_verify`) while
    the run reads. The check stops when the run ends, so it never makes the run longer.
  - **Refuted.** If the verdict comes back *refuted*, pysacd warns clearly: the frames before
    the frame from which reading was exact again may differ from an exact read, so run again
    with `--exact`. The exit status is then 1. A sector source (a PS3) can't be read from two
    threads, so a provisional start from one is logged as not checked.
  - **`--exact`** (`pysacd-extract`, `pysacd convert`) reads the area up to the range, as a
    straight read does.
  - **Tested.** `tests/test_engine_scarletbook.py` compares provisional and exact reads of every
    track of every hostile image (`seek_min_gap=0`, so every range is provisional): same bytes,
    or both fail, and none refuted. The harness's range modes do the same on real discs.

### Output through scarletbook

Since 0.4.0, every byte of a DSF or DSDIFF file that isn't audio comes from scarletbook's output
API (#94): `src/pysacd/sbwriter.py` asks scarletbook 0.5.4 for each file's layout from the TOC
(`sb_output_layout_new`, `sb_output_layout_new_dst`, `sb_output_dsf_chain_plan`) and the engine
writes its header and trailer around the audio it streams. pysacd's own DSF header writer and
DSDIFF chunk writer are deleted. The owner's rule for offloading is to adopt scarletbook where
the output is byte-identical and no more than 15 % slower, and then delete pysacd's own code;
both hold (see [performance](performance.md)).

- **The writer's choices** that give `sacd_extract`'s bytes, all in scarletbook 0.5.4
  (scarletbook-rs#169):
  - DSF: the tag is passed as the raw tag, ID3v2.4 or v2.3 (`sb_output_options_set_raw_tag`),
    or none; an area of unspecified layout gets `sacd_extract`'s channel type by channel count.
  - DSF without padding (`-z`): the selected tracks whose ranges meet end to end form one
    chain (`sb_output_dsf_chain_plan`, options 37 and 38). Every file but the area's last track
    ends on a whole block, and the bytes left over open the next file. When the last selected
    track isn't the area's last, the chain runs one frame past it, so that its file ends
    unpadded too, as `sacd_extract`'s does.
  - DSDIFF: `DIIN` with `DIAR` and `DITI`, their pad byte counted; `DSTI` offsets at the frame
    data; `LSCO` 65 535 for an unspecified layout; local chunks in `sacd_extract`'s order. A
    track file has no `EMID` (option 33) and takes `DIAR` and `DITI` from its track, or else
    from the album (option 34); an edited master keeps an empty `EMID`. Departures D1 (`CMPR`
    of plain DSD counts its pad byte) and D2 (text as ISO 8859-1) are named: they make files
    that don't conform to DSDIFF, and `sacd_extract` writes them.
- **What stays pysacd's is content, not layout:** the ID3 tag `sacd_extract` makes from the TOC
  (`sbcompat.id3_tag`), which goes in as a DSF file's raw tag and as a DSDIFF file's `ID3 `
  caller chunks (padded to even length, with the pad counted, as `sacd_extract` counts it), and
  `sacd_extract`'s markers and `COMT` comments, passed as the caller's own. scarletbook's own
  tag from the TOC (`sb_tags_from_toc`) is another tag: `sacd_extract` writes `TYER` and
  `TDAT`, a `TXXX` performer and ID3v1 genre names.
- **DST files are finished after the run.** Their frames' lengths are known only once they
  are read, so the engine writes a header of the right length, then the frames, and
  `extract.finish_dff` loads the lengths (`sb_dst_lengths_load`) and writes scarletbook's
  header and trailer.
- **Checked.** After each DSF and plain DSD DSDIFF file, its size must be the layout's; a DST
  file's frames must fill the layout's sound data exactly. A file that fails the check is
  deleted and the run exits with 255.
- **What scarletbook refuses isn't written.** A file of a hostile or damaged TOC that
  scarletbook won't lay out (an empty track, a range past the area or its capacity, an
  impossible date, an unsupported channel count) is reported, not written, and the run exits
  with 255. pysacd 0.3 wrote such files from the TOC as it stood. No real disc in the tests has
  one.
- **Unreadable frames in a DST file.** `sacd_extract` leaves them out of the file. The layout is
  then made for the frames the file holds, so the file is as before, except that a marker past
  them (the index marker at a track's end, or an edited master's later markers) can't be
  written: it is left out. This happens only on a damaged image.

**Checking the outputs.** `tools/extract_compare.py` runs `pysacd-extract` and `pysacd convert`
in 35 modes with two pysacd source trees, and the `sacd_extract`-compatible modes with
`sacd_extract` as a black box. The modes cover DSF, DSDIFF with DST kept or decoded, the edit
master alone and with DSF (one pass), cue and XML, pauses, no padding, single tracks, the ISO copy alone and with DSF,
concatenation, multichannel, `-P`, FLAC, WAV at 176.4 kHz, `convert` with and without
pauses, and the writer's choices of #94 one by one (ID3 modes 0 to 5, `-z` on a selection and
with pauses, DSDIFF with pauses, a multichannel edited master). The new tree must give the same files, names and bytes as the old one, and must match
`sacd_extract` file by file wherever the old one did. `--no-values` reports counts only.

**Moving to another scarletbook release:**

1. Download its `scarletbook-ffi-*` assets, check each with `sha256sum -c` and
   `gh attestation verify <file> -R aclater/scarletbook-rs`, and read its changelog.
2. Update `version`, `commit` and every digest in `scarletbook.lock`. If the C ABI changed, also
   update `abi`, the check in `csrc/sacdconv.c` and `SB_ABI` in `_native.py`, and port the
   code that calls it.
3. Update the versions of the Rust crates in `licenses/scarletbook-rs-runtime-MIT` if they
   changed (scarletbook's `Cargo.lock`).

**Licence.** scarletbook-rs, and the Rust standard library and crates inside it, are licensed
MIT OR Apache-2.0. pysacd uses them under MIT, which is compatible with GPL-2.0; Apache-2.0
isn't. Their notices ship in every wheel and the sdist (`licenses/`).

**Hardening.** Since scarletbook-rs 0.5.2, every object in its x86-64 Linux library carries the
CET shadow-stack (SHSTK) property (scarletbook-rs#125), so the engine is SHSTK-marked again, as it
was up to 0.2.2: a process running with shadow stacks can load it. 0.3.0, linked with 0.5.1, had
no CET mark (a library is marked only when every object in it is). Indirect branch tracking (IBT)
stays unmarked: stable Rust's standard library has no `ENDBR64`. `tools/check_cet.py` checks the
mark with `readelf -n`, in CI on the engine and on the x86-64 manylinux wheel after auditwheel
(#94). The musllinux engine stays unmarked: Alpine's startup objects (`crti.o`, `crtbeginS.o`)
have no CET property, and musl never turns shadow stacks on, so the mark would change nothing. The other hardening properties are unchanged: full RELRO, `BIND_NOW` and a
non-executable stack. See [performance](performance.md#hardening).

## Tests

```
make && PYTHONPATH=src python3 -m unittest discover -s tests
PYSACD_TEST_ISO=/path/to/disc.iso PYTHONPATH=src python3 -m unittest discover -s tests
```

With `SACD_EXTRACT=/path/to/sacd_extract` and `PYSACD_TEST_ISO` set, the tests also
copy the ISO through `ps3sim` with the real `sacd_extract -I` and check that the copy
is byte-identical.

`tests/test_fuzz.py` feeds seeded, mutated input to the protocol decoder, the PS3 client,
the TOC reader and the `ps3sim` handler. It runs 300 cases per target by default;
`PYSACD_FUZZ=5000` runs more. A failure names the seed that reproduces it.

The engine has a libFuzzer harness in `fuzz/`, `fuzz_engine`. It needs clang. Each input is a
disc image: the harness opens it with scarletbook and runs `sacdconv_area_run()` on each area,
as the commands do:
- the whole area, capped at 600 frames, to DSF, DSDIFF and, for a DST area, DSDIFF with the
  stored frames, in one pass;
- the last track to WAV, through a sector source and with a provisional start.

scarletbook's own parsing is fuzzed in its repository; this covers pysacd's code around it.

```sh
make fuzz test-tools
PYTHONPATH=src:tests python3 fuzz/make_seeds.py build/fuzz-seeds
build/fuzz_engine -max_len=4194304 -jobs=8 -workers=8 -max_total_time=600 build/fuzz-corpus/engine build/fuzz-seeds/engine
```

The seeds are pysacd's hostile corpus (`tests/sacdgen.py`) and DST discs built by the test
encoder. A crashing input goes, minimised, into `fuzz/regressions/fuzz_engine/` along with its
fix. `tests/test_fuzz_engine.py` builds the same harness without libFuzzer (`make
fuzz-replay`, any C compiler) and replays those inputs and the seeds, under the sanitizers
in CI.

To report a vulnerability, see [SECURITY.md](../SECURITY.md).

## CI

Every pull request runs:

- **ruff and mypy** on the Python code.
- **The test suite** on Python 3.11 to 3.14, with the engine built with
  `-Werror` (FLAC included).
- **The tests under AddressSanitizer and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer**, and again under
  **ThreadSanitizer**.
- **libFuzzer** on the engine (`fuzz_engine`), 2 minutes, when `csrc/`, `fuzz/`, the
  hostile corpus or the scarletbook pin changes. A weekly run lasts 30 minutes and keeps its
  corpus cached.
- **The comparison tests** against a `sacd_extract` built from a pinned
  upstream commit inside the runner. Its code never enters the repository.
- **CodeQL** (Python, C, workflows) and **semgrep**.
- **A check for private names**, in files and commit identities.
- **scarletbook provenance**: every archive pinned in `scarletbook.lock` must match its digest
  and carry a valid build provenance attestation from scarletbook-rs's release workflow, for the
  pinned tag and commit (see [the scarletbook library](#the-scarletbook-library)).
- **zizmor**, the GitHub Actions security linter, when `.github/workflows/` changes
  (offline audits; run it locally with
  `pipx run zizmor==1.30.1 --no-online-audits .github/workflows`).
- **Dependency review**: a pull request that adds a dependency with a known high or
  critical vulnerability fails.
- **Coverage**: the Python 3.13 leg runs the suite under coverage.py (settings in
  `pyproject.toml`) and shows the report in the job summary, with the HTML and XML
  reports as the `coverage` artifact. The XML report also goes to
  [Codecov](https://codecov.io/gh/aclater/pysacd) for the README badge, authenticated
  with the job's GitHub OIDC token (no stored secret); pull requests from forks skip
  the upload, and a failed upload fails CI only on `master`.
- **A link check** (lychee) of README.md and `docs/` when they change.
- **An AI review** from a second model, using PR-Agent. It needs the
  `GEMINI_API_KEY` repository secret. **This sends each PR's title,
  description and diff to Google's Gemini API**, a third party, even though
  the repository is private. Without the secret the workflow sends nothing.

Scheduled runs, besides the weekly fuzzing and portability runs:

- **OpenSSF Scorecard**, weekly and on every push to master. The results are published
  (the README badge) and appear under code scanning.
- **A live MusicBrainz lookup**, weekly (or by hand from the Actions tab): the test suite
  mocks MusicBrainz, so `tests/test_musicbrainz_live.py` makes one real request through
  pysacd's client, to notice when the API stops fitting the parser. It skips unless
  `PYSACD_LIVE_MB=1`; run it locally with
  `PYSACD_LIVE_MB=1 PYTHONPATH=src pytest tests/test_musicbrainz_live.py`.
- **The link check**, weekly, since links rot without a code change.

CI installs its Python dependencies with every package pinned and hash-checked
(`pip install --require-hashes`):

- `requirements-dev.txt` holds everything: test dependencies, linters, `build` and the build backend;
- `requirements-test.txt` holds only what the tests need, for the Windows and fuzz jobs.

CI installs pysacd itself with `--no-build-isolation`, so nothing unhashed is downloaded; the
release workflow's sdist is built the same way, with `build` from `requirements-dev.txt`. To
update a pin, edit `PINS` in `tools/lock_dev.py` and run `python3 -I tools/lock_dev.py`. It
rewrites both files from PyPI's hashes and refuses releases younger than two weeks, except
versions already in the lock (Dependabot bumps the lock files directly, after its cooldown).
For local work, `pip install -e '.[dev]'` still works. Dependabot keeps the SHA-pinned actions
and the locked packages current, with a two-week cooldown.

Contributor rules (clean room, byte-identity, benchmarks, privacy) are in [CLAUDE.md](../CLAUDE.md).

## Testing without a PS3

`pysacd ps3sim` serves an ISO over the SACD Ripper protocol, so the network
client (and `sacd_extract -i`) can be tested without a PS3. It can throttle,
add latency, drop connections and fail reads on demand:

```console
$ pysacd ps3sim album.iso --port 2002 --rate 6 --drop-after 500
serving album.iso as a SACD Ripper server on 127.0.0.1:2002 (Ctrl-C to stop)
```

It's a test tool, not a way to share discs: the protocol has no
authentication. See [PS3 network protocol](ps3-protocol.md#testing-without-a-ps3) for how
faithful it is.

## Packaging and releases

`setup.py` builds the engine while building the package, in a private
directory, so your `build/` and `src/pysacd/_sacdconv.so` are left alone. The
engine is a ctypes library rather than a CPython extension, so one
`py3-none-<platform>` wheel serves every Python version.

`.github/workflows/workflow.yml` builds wheels for manylinux (x86-64, aarch64),
musllinux (x86-64), macOS (arm64, x86-64) and Windows (x86-64), plus the sdist,
whenever packaging or `csrc/` changes. Every wheel's engine has the pinned scarletbook library
linked in statically, and the wheel job runs only after the `scarletbook provenance` check.
auditwheel and delocate bundle libFLAC and libogg; the Windows DLL is linked statically. Their licences ship in the wheel
(`licenses/`). Every wheel, and a build from the sdist, runs `tests/wheel_smoke.py`
in a clean environment: it converts a synthetic disc to DSF and FLAC with the
installed console scripts, and checks that the engine has the pinned scarletbook release
(version and commit) linked in. Building from the sdist downloads that release, as `make` does. Runtime SIMD dispatch needs glibc, so musllinux wheels
use the plain filters.

To release:

1. Bump `version` in `pyproject.toml` and `src/pysacd/__init__.py`, and merge.
2. Tag `vX.Y.Z` on master and push the tag. The workflow then:
   - creates build provenance attestations for every wheel and the sdist;
   - attaches the files to a GitHub release, each with its attestation bundle as
     `<file>.intoto.jsonl` (verified in the job first). Check a download with
     `gh attestation verify <file> --repo aclater/pysacd`, adding
     `--bundle <file>.intoto.jsonl` to check against the attached bundle. OpenSSF
     Scorecard counts only these assets as provenance;
   - publishes to TestPyPI, if the repository variable `TESTPYPI_PUBLISH` is
     `true` (trusted publishing, environment `testpypi`);
   - then publishes to PyPI, if `PYPI_PUBLISH` is `true` (environment `pypi`),
     and only if TestPyPI succeeded or was skipped.
3. Trusted publishing is configured once per index on its website: owner
   `aclater`, repository `pysacd`, workflow `workflow.yml`, environment `pypi`
   (the PyPI publisher is constrained to it). On GitHub, the `pypi` environment
   only accepts `v*` tags, so nothing but a release tag can publish. No API token
   is stored anywhere.

## CI speed

A pull request's checks finish in about 3 min, and a new push cancels the superseded run (`concurrency`; master runs are never cancelled). The test matrix caches pip downloads. Every required check runs on every pull request: none is path-filtered at the workflow level, because a skipped required check stays pending and blocks the merge. Keep new jobs short, and put slow, rarely-failing ones on master, tags or a schedule.
